items.title: Agent Distraction
items.summary: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. In 6% of encounters, agents act on these comments, with 83% being entirely unprompted by the developer. These detours result in significant overhead—adding 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, and 105% more wait time per session—split between chasing closed tickets (41%) and unauthorized scope creep on open bugs (57%). Higher-capability models show higher distraction rates, highlighting the need for automated cleanup and linters to maintain agent-friendly codebases

By decoupling model definition from physical hardware via virtual devices, developers can efficiently scale complex training architectures and seamlessly handle dynamic workloads like reinforcement learning post-training.

items.title: Node.js Support Pool — Failed Webhook Tasks Need an Idempotent Consumer

Short answer: use a standard queue with explicit ack/nack handling, send poison messages to a dead-letter queue (DLQ), and make the Node.js consumer idempotent before redriving failed jobs. Delivery is at-least-once, so retry safety belongs in the consumer, not in wishful queue settings. The recommendation is deliberately narrow. Its consistent interface under one key also lowers the integration work when the same support system needs other backend capabilities. The queue design still matters more than the vendor. A generation retry can consume more model or accelerator work; a transfer retry should usually resend one part. Keeping those paths separate also keeps long-lived storage authority out of a browser or image worker. Start with two actors. The trusted API chooses the bucket and object key, binds them to a tenant and image job, starts the multipart session, and issues a presigned URL for one numbered part at a time. The worker holds the bytes, uploads each part, retains the response ETag, and asks the API to finalize or cancel. It does not choose a new key halfway through the transfer. AWS describes a presigned URL as a way to grant time-limited access without giving the recipient storage credentials. items.title: Feature Flags Service: Safe Notification Toggles and Rollback Explained
items.summary: Use a feature flag to return a failing notification service to its previous delivery path, and verify delivery outcomes before declaring the rollback complete. items.title: Why your calculator's money math is wrong (and how to fix it)
items.summary: If you have ever built a loan or mortgage calculator, you have probably shipped this bug: 0.1 + 0.2 in JavaScript is 0.30000000000000004, not 0.3. Display it raw and your calculator tells a user their payment is $313.36000000000003. Round only at display time and the error compounds across an amortisation schedule, so the final balance comes out a few cents off and the schedule never quite reaches zero. Three rules that fix it in practice: Do money in integer cents (or a decimal type) until the very last step. Parse the input once, convert dollars to cents, and keep every intermediate value in cents. Only format back to dollars for display. Round each month's split, not just the total. Interest for a month is balance x monthly rate, rounded to the cent; principal is payment minus that rounded interest. If you round only the payment, the schedule drifts. Force the last payment to clear the balance. Take a $10,000 loan at 8% over 3 years: the payment is $313.36 a month, first month's interest is $66.67 and the total interest is $1,281.09. The usual answer is credits: sell a "500 credit pack", price clips in credits, let credits expire. I don't like credits. items.title: Day 21: Business Logic Customization and the Four Plugin Stages
items.summary: Multilingual Customization and Resource Structure ended on a situation where the difference one company wants is too large for language resources or layouts to hold. Requests of that kind have a different shape from the two posts before: one more credit limit check before a save, a document synchronized to another system after a save, a notice to the warehouse on a delete. What they want is not a definition that reads differently, it is a piece of behavior that runs. The framework already has a route for that: inherit the whole form's business object and swap the binding in the registry. But that route is too heavy for the three things above. Sending one notification after a save means taking over the business object for the entire document. Three unrelated customizations stacked together can only be written into the same subclass. And whether logic the package adds to that step later still runs at all depends on whether the subclass remembered to call base. What is missing is not an extension point, it is a way to hook in that weighs less than inheritance and can be declared per customization. items.title: Stitching Photos into One Long Image in Swift: Common Width, a Height Cap, and One Photo in Memory at a Time
items.summary: A long image is the simplest way to post a set of photos as one thing: a trip, a recipe, a product from every angle. Stack the photos top to bottom, export one file, done. The first version most of us write is also simple: load every photo as a UIImage, add up the heights, draw them into a UIGraphicsImageRenderer, save. It works on the simulator with five screenshots. Then someone picks twelve 48-megapixel photos, two of them shot sideways, and the app either dies or produces a 9,000 × 60,000 pixel file that no social app will show at full size. I build BatchMark, an on-device photo app for iPhone, and its Photo Stories feature joins a set of finished photos into one long image. This post is a teaching extract of the problems you hit when you build that kind of stitcher, not the app's source. Everything here is ImageIO and Core Graphics, no third-party code. The approach has four parts: Read each photo's pixel size without decoding it. Plan the layout: one common width, heights scaled to match, total height capped. items.title: Build Buddy, after the week: I tested my own fix on new samples
items.summary: Builders Week is over, but a reader's suggestion left one question open. Quick recap: Build Buddy asks a local Gemma 3 4B to fix C# compiler errors, then checks each fix by rebuilding and running the program. A fix only counts if it builds and prints the expected output. On my six samples, Gemma scored 5/6. The one failure was CS0161: the fix compiled, but added two extra Console.WriteLine calls. A reader suggested treating that as a known failure case and changing the prompt. One sentence, "Keep the program's behaviour and console output exactly the same," took it to 6/6. I wrote the rule after seeing the six samples fail, and I tested it on the same six. That's the classic way to fool yourself. A fix tuned on the test can pass the test without being any good. So I added four new samples the rule had never seen, each with one planted error and an expected.txt. I checked every answer key by running a hand-written correct fix first, because on Day 1 one of my own test cases was broken. Held-out sample Planted error Should print unassigned local CS0165: total used before it's set 12 max missing return CS0161: Max doesn't always return 7 int to bool CS0029: an int used as a bool True

items.title: Initialize Once, Hydrate Deliberately: Choosing a FeatureCell's Starting State
items.summary: A FeatureCell does not start with "whatever was in the constructor." Calling initialize() activates the runtime pipeline, and the value it begins with depends on a resolved decision between a declared default, a previously persisted value, and a deliberate hydrate() factory. Knowing which source wins — and why — is what separates an accidental starting value from an intentional one. This post walks through what initialize() actually activates, when hydrate() overrides everything else, and how to choose between a static default, Persist behaviors, and an explicit factory when your FeatureCell comes online. Key takeaway: Initialization is not a direct mutation. Whatever value is selected — hydrated, persisted, or declared — is enqueued as a replaceState operation and processed through the same pipeline as any other update. A FeatureCell is not operational the moment it is declared. It becomes a runtime participant only after initialize() is called — once, and exactly once. items.title: Typed Verification Timelines for React Forms
items.summary: Email verification looks like a small form feature: collect an address, send a code, and show a success message. In a real product, it is a timeline with several actors: the browser, the API, the mail provider, a user who may open two tabs, and a timer that eventually expires. When those actors disagree, a React component often falls back to a handful of booleans: const [loading, setLoading] = useState(false) const [verified, setVerified] = useState(false) const [error, setError] = useState (null) This works for the happy path. It gets confusing when a resend request finishes after an old verification request, or when a user returns to a tab after the code has expired. A typed timeline makes the UI easier to reason about and gives tests something more useful than a screenshot to assert. loading, verified, and error can all be true at the same time. That means the component can accidentally render “Verified” while a newer request is still pending. The UI should not guess what the API mean; it should render a state that already explains the server decision. This time it's the European Accessibility Act, or the EAA for short. The GDPR has been around since 2018, but the EAA is still pretty new. Its rules started to apply on 28 June 2025, and a lot of teams only started taking action for it very recently. Accessibility is a topic that's very close to my heart. I've given talks about the EAA at .NET conferences and JS conferences, and this post is the written version of that story for .NET developers. Less Vue, more Razor and Blazor. If your company sells a lot to consumers in the EU, or you're not sure if the law applies to you, talk to a legal professional or an accessibility auditor. The EAA (Directive (EU) 2019/882) is a European law that makes sure people with disabilities can use the same products and services as everyone else. items.title: Mozilla to Shut Down Solo, Deleting Users' Websites and Data
items.summary: Mozilla is shutting down Solo, its AI-powered website builder and hosting service, on November 30. A notice on the Soloist.ai homepage reads: "We've made the difficult decision to close Solo. We have appreciated all of your support building and growing this product, and the feedback we've received from all of you. Solo will cease operations on Nov 30, 2026." The Register reports: Mozilla launched Solo in December 2023 as a "Mozilla Innovation Project," aimed at helping sole traders to build themselves a webpage for their services. Some 54,000 people used its LLM to build pages, and relied on Mozilla to host them -- complete with custom domain names. Users now have just over two weeks left to find a new home for their pages, although Mozilla says it first notified them on October 1. According to the support FAQ, users can download a ZIP containing an HTML export, contact form and newsletter submissions, and a CSV linking to their images. The images themselves must be downloaded separately. Domains purchased through Solo Domains must also be moved to Name.com, with Mozilla handling the transfer after users create an account and supply its code. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

El escaneo de vulnerabilidades busca fallas de seguridad conocidas antes de que el código llegue a producción. Las herramientas SAST revisan el código fuente sin ejecutarlo y señalan patrones riesgosos: algoritmos criptográficos débiles, credenciales escritas en el código o conexiones sin cifrar. Elegí DevSkim porque figura en la lista de herramientas de escaneo de vulnerabilidades de OWASP, es gratuito y de código abierto, soporta C# y otros lenguajes, y genera resultados en formato SARIF, el estándar que GitHub entiende de forma nativa. La aplicación de ejemplo es Banco API, una Minimal API en .NET 8 con endpoints para consultar saldos, generar hashes y tokens. Incluí vulnerabilidades intencionales para que DevSkim tenga qué encontrar. Repositorio público del equipo: github.com/viccarretero/banco-api-vulnerabilidades. items.title: Letting an AI assistant read SQL Server without letting it write
items.summary: The problem The request sounds simple: let an AI assistant answer questions from a company's on-premises SQL Server. The hard part is what the assistant must not be able to do. The threat model treats the assistant itself as the attacker: it can be prompt-injected, for example by text stored in a table it just read, or simply make a mistake. The goal is that three things still hold: it cannot change the database, it cannot read outside the connected database, and it cannot get data back from a call before that call is recorded. First, what no gateway fixes: the rows the assistant reads leave the building, to the AI vendor that runs the model. Read-only does not change that. What may be sent, under which personal-data rules (KVKK in Turkey, others elsewhere), is the firm's decision. mssql-readonly-mcp is a free, open-source (MIT) MCP server in C# on .NET 10. The assistant's client starts it as a local stdio process. It offers three tools: list_tables, describe_table and run_query. Only run_query takes SQL. items.title: The Old Screen Was the Real Spec: Rewriting a Streaming Portal From AngularJS to React
items.summary: Rewriting a legacy frontend is usually described as a coding problem. It almost never is. It is a specification problem wearing a coding problem's clothes, and the teams that get this wrong ship a different, undocumented application instead of a modernized version of the one operators already trust. Here is how a streaming operations portal came off AngularJS and onto React without breaking the people who use it every day. Dense, long lived screens. Driven by asynchronous backend jobs. items.title: Implementing In-Memory Caching in Azure Logic Apps Standard Using C#
items.summary: When building enterprise integration solutions using Azure Logic Apps Standard, we sometimes need to retrieve the same reference or configuration information repeatedly during workflow execution. If every workflow execution performs the same lookup operation, it can introduce unnecessary processing, increase response time and create additional dependencies on external systems. One way to address this is by implementing in-memory caching using C# within Azure Logic Apps Standard. In this article, I'll explain how we can use a custom C# workflow action and IMemoryCache to store frequently accessed information and reuse it across workflow executions.

Both release notes are public, and they are the source for every DraftKey detail in this post. We build DraftKey, a Mac app for Tab autocomplete and rewrites you review before they are inserted. Someone installs a writing helper on a Monday, uses it twice, gets busy, and comes back on day 15 to a locked app they never really tried. items.title: Volume zero is not mute
items.summary: With the volume at zero, my MacBook's speakers were still playing. Quietly enough that you only notice in a quiet room, but they were playing. On a Mac, volume and mute are two separate things. Volume is a number between 0 and 1. Mute is a switch. CoreAudio keeps them as two properties on the output device, and nothing forces them to agree. The number is a position on the device's range, and the device reports that range in decibels. So I asked the built-in speakers for theirs: var range = AudioValueRange() var size = UInt32(MemoryLayout .size) var a = AudioObjectPropertyAddress( mSelector: kAudioDevicePropertyVolumeRangeDecibels, mScope: kAudioDevicePropertyScopeOutput, mElement: kAudioObjectPropertyElementMain) AudioObjectGetPropertyData(device, &a, 0, nil, &size, &range) print(range.mMinimum, range.mMaximum) // -63.5 0.0 The bottom of the range is −63.5 dB. That is very quiet. It is not off. Usually nobody notices, because macOS flips the mute switch as well when the volume arrives at zero. items.title: Why a Mac Writing Helper Needs Two Permissions, and Why It Still Refuses Password Fields
items.summary: A writing helper that works inside someone else's text field has to ask macOS for a lot of trust. Accessibility permission is how an app reads and, if you approve it, replaces text in another app. Input Monitoring is how it can see keyboard events while you are in Mail, Notes, or a browser. Those are two different Privacy & Security toggles, and they should be. People are right to pause on both. We build DraftKey, a Mac app for Tab autocomplete and rewrites you review before they are inserted. This post is about the permission model behind a helper like that: why two system permissions are required, how we ask for them, and the cases we refuse even after you have said yes. The general mechanics come from Apple's public documentation, linked at the end. The product rules come from the shipped app's own wording, including the Apps & privacy section in Settings. Apple documents these as separate resources, and System Settings treats them that way. Accessibility is under Privacy & Security. items.title: Monolith, Modular Monolith and Microservices: A Practical Comparison for .NET
items.summary: Cover photo by Nicolás Gutiérrez on Unsplash Most software engineers do not choose their architecture in a vacuum. You usually meet architectures in stages: traditional monoliths in legacy codebases or early-stage products, microservices when a company wants independent team scaling, and modular monoliths when an organization realizes that distributed systems introduce operational costs they did not anticipate. Each approach is often marketed as the obvious successor to the one before it. In real engineering, however, these architectures are simply points on a trade-off spectrum balancing operational simplicity against structural isolation. This article compares traditional monoliths, modular monoliths, and microservices across core architectural dimensions, outlines the specific .NET libraries and frameworks each one relies on, and provides practical criteria for choosing between them. If you ship a Mac app outside the App Store, most of this applies to you whatever updater you use. Desktop apps break in different places: the clipboard, designer resources, third-party controls, installers and Office add-ins. Here is the checklist I use for WinForms and WPF apps, roughly in the order things go wrong. Open each .csproj and look at the target: net8.0-windows or net9.0-windows: affected, keep reading. v4.x : this is .NET Framework. It is not affected by this deadline, because .NET Framework 4.8.1 is supported as part of Windows. Moving to .NET 10 is still worth it, but it is a bigger project (see step 8). Run dotnet --list-runtimes on a typical user machine too. You will often find several runtimes installed that nobody remembers adding. A framework-dependent .NET 8 app will not start on the .NET 10 runtime by default. If you can't migrate this month, you can let it run on a newer major version: Major This is a stopgap, not a migration. items.summary: 👉 Full lesson with practice questions on DevLadder (free, lesson 2 of 15 in the OOP Concepts in C# course) public class Logger { public static readonly DateTime LoadedAt; static Logger() { LoadedAt = DateTime.UtcNow; } // static ctor: once per type, before first use public string Name { get; } public Logger() : this("default") { } // chaining to another ctor public Logger(string name) { Name = name; } } public class Settings { private Settings() { } // private ctor: no outside 'new' public static Settings Load() => new Settings(); // factory method / Singleton } public class Admin : User { public Admin(string email) : base(email) { } // call base constructor } If you write no constructor, C# provides a parameterless one. Writing any constructor removes it. Order: static fields → static ctor (once) → instance field initialisers → base ctor → derived ctor body. The 21-year-old computer science major helped collect hundreds of signatures earlier this year from students, faculty, alumni and residents to demand that Stanford drop its current Flock contract and codify safeguards for similar tech tools the school may use in the future. The fear, Nguyen says, is that these cameras, which show where a vehicle was at a certain point in time, can be exploited to victimize vulnerable people. Stanford cut ties with Flock this summer, and it’s not alone. The privacy reckoning over the company’s surveillance cameras is gaining momentum at schools nationwide. Since April, at least ten university campuses across seven states, have scrapped contracts with Flock. items.title: FAA Expands AI Advice to Manage Air Traffic Congestion Across Entire US Airspace
items.summary: The FAA is expanding its $875 million AI-powered SMART system to all 22 U.S. air traffic control centers across the country. Since being implemented over Washington, DC, on September 21, the system has helped reroute 180 flights, saving an average of 10 minutes and nearly 80 gallons of fuel per flight. Ars Technica reports: The FAA fact sheet describes SMART as a cloud-based system that combines information about "weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow and controller staffing metrics" to predict air traffic patterns. It is designed to make scheduling recommendations, identify optimal flight routes, and determine the best order of arrivals for aircraft. However, a human team of FAA specialists based in DC is ultimately responsible for validating the SMART system recommendations before passing them along to air traffic control facilities across the country, according to the agency. Furthermore, the AI-powered SMART system "cannot be used to replace the critical role air traffic controllers play or take over control of an aircraft," the FAA clarified in the September 21 announcement about the initial deployment. "The mission's goal is to complete the "largest-ever three-dimensional atlas of the cosmos, spanning more than a third of the sky, in 2031." From the report: "It marks a major milestone for ESA's Euclid mission and for everyone involved," said astrophysicist Valeria Pettorino, ESA's Euclid project scientist. Euclid, launched from Florida in 2023, is gathering data on how the universe has expanded and how its structure has formed over time while amassing information about the nature of dark energy and dark matter and the role of gravity on large scales. "Euclid will not just take images of galaxies in the sky, in two dimensions, but will also measure their distance, the third dimension. items.title: What it takes to turn an iPhone microphone into a decibel meter
items.summary: I work on Noise Meter at W Lab. It is an iPhone app that shows the sound level in decibels and logs a whole night of it, so someone with a noisy neighbour can show when it was loud. This post is about the measuring part: what happens between the microphone and the number on screen, and the places where I had to be honest about what a phone can't do. iOS processes microphone input by default: automatic gain, noise suppression, EQ. All of that is exactly what a meter must not have, because a quiet room would be boosted and a loud one pulled down. The audio session mode that turns it off is .measurement: try session.setCategory(.record, mode: .measurement) try session.setPreferredSampleRate(48_000) From there it is an AVAudioEngine input tap with a 4800-frame buffer, which is 100 ms at 48 kHz. I ask for 48 kHz but build the analyzer for whatever rate the hardware returns. I also select the built-in microphone's bottom data source with an omnidirectional pattern, and re-select it on every route change, because a route change can move the input. items.title: Datacentres are deeply unpopular. Has Sweden made one we can all love?
items.summary: It is built of wood, resembles an Ikea and its power is totally renewable. Plus, it was built with the local community in mind. Is this facility in Falun the best datacentre in the world? ‘It was pretty cool, when they were building it. It looked like a very large Ikea,” says John Wernvik, of EcoDataCenter. He is giving me a tour of their facility in Falun, Sweden, which could lay claim to being the world’s greenest datacentre – although to many, that is a contradiction in terms. One difference is immediately visible: this datacentre is made out of wood. Huge panels of cross-laminated timber arrived at the site pre-cut, and were assembled by crane according to instructions, like flatpack furniture. Aesthetically, this section of the datacentre is more like an Ikea before the fit-out, a cavernous, echoey, immaculately clean hangar. items.title: Tanuki: Pon’s Summer review – an adorable raccoon mends the world, one parcel at a time
items.summary: Nintendo Switch/2, PlayStation 4/5, Xbox One/series X/S, PC; Denkiworks/Inpleron Limited This gentle game of fixing and fetching, in which you play as a furry post office worker on a BMX, has a slow, calming magic that delights in routine and restoration Arriving alongside November’s blue wave, Tanuki: Pon’s Summer is a game of quiet restoration that feels perfectly suited to the current moment. Tasked with repairing an ancient shrine in the weeks leading up to a local festival, you’ll find yourself cleaning out trash, mending broken arches and slowly bringing a small rural community back together. It sounds a bit like JL Carr’s compact but enchanting novel A Month in the Country, except instead of shell-shocked veterans of the first world war you’re left exploring the rich inner life of a Japanese racoon dog who can ride a BMX. Even so, the mixture of steady progress and general low stakes proves intoxicating. This is a short game, but it’s hard not to linger over it. Continue reading...

items.title: Handing over humanity (22 minute read)
items.summary: Some AI experts believe that once we achieve superintelligence, humans will be permanently disempowered, and we shall all be ruled by an AI god. This might not be such a desirable outcome, as humans have a natural desire for freedom. The arrangement will probably not work, as keeping power responsive to human needs has required checks developed over centuries, sustained by repeated feedback from the real world and correction, and there's no reason to keep that equilibrium stable once humans have surrendered all control. Humans have the ability now to steer the technology in a way that will not lead to a complete replacement of human judgment.

items.title: What objective is reasoning solving? (12 minute read)
items.summary: Reasoning is pathfinding in token space. There are many paths from the problem to a correct answer, and the model traverses each of them with each sample. A path is not guaranteed to converge to the correct answer - it's only in aggregate, over the distribution of paths, do we get a high probability of success. RL training directly raises the success probability. The gains credited to 'thinking longer' come from the search paid for during training rather than at inference.

items.title: Two Kinds of Test-Time Scaling (28 minute read)
items.summary: Test-time scaling trades compute for performance at test time. There are two types of test-time scaling: one allows researchers to trade more compute for more performance per task, but only up to the maximum quantity of per-task compute used during training; and the other lets researchers trade more compute for more performance per task, and lets them do so up to quantities of compute and performance that never occurred during training. Scaling methods that permit the latter change will have a larger impact than test-time scaling considered simply. This essay describes how this may impact the world.

items.title: Harness 2: executing agent code as it streams (6 minute read)
items.summary: Framer's Harness 2 significantly upgrades the agent's execution process, allowing entire workflows in one program, achieving up to 33% cost reduction and 20% faster execution. This is done by executing JavaScript as it streams in, avoiding multiple model calls and using eager execution and early cancellation to enhance efficiency. The redesign also replaces DSL with method calls for real-time updates, making task execution streamlined for both in-app and external agents, reducing tool steps by 43% and cached input tokens by 39% per message.

items.title: How to Train a Swarm (19 minute read)
items.summary: Swarms are AI systems where multiple agents cooperate towards a shared goal. This post discusses a technique called collective inference-time scaling, where agents scale the amount of useful work performed in parallel and the communication needed to achieve it. It also explains how to design incentives for parallel work, and covers the general topic of designing incentives for reinforcement learning.

items.title: Why Agents Are Soon Only Going to Have 1 Tool (9 minute read)
items.summary: Agents are collapsing their entire tool catalog into one 'exec' tool. This allows models to write short scripts that chain, combine, and await actions inside isolated sandboxes. Models can now reliably combine and chain dependent actions in a single pass. In the previous standard tool-calling model, agents could only perform single actions, but the exec tool allows them to perform multiple actions.

items.title: What Is Quantum Advantage Actually Worth? (9 minute read)

items.title: Scaling Git at OpenAI (31 minute read)
items.summary: OpenAI's monorepo's size and demands increased at a staggering pace over the last year, necessitating a revamp of the AI lab's source control system. Its technical staff built Pando, a new backend for Git repositories optimized for concurrent pushes to many branches and to maximize read throughput. The team implemented the backend without interrupting any engineering work or changing how the team uses Git. Pando cut median push latency in production by nearly 5x, and it now delivers nearly a petabyte of Git data per day.

items.title: Lessons from building Copilot Cowork (21 minute read)
items.summary: Microsoft's Copilot Cowork, an AI-driven agentic execution layer, achieved global availability in four and a half months, switching its runtime from Python to Rust while live. Key practices included writing clear specs before coding, running narrow agents with clear boundaries, and ensuring automated checks genuinely verify code changes. The transition to Rust improved efficiency and highlighted the importance of clear testing, boundary setting, and human oversight in the development process.
